title: 0460-rethinking-evaluation-metric-for-probability-estimation
universal_lens: The Balance score defines a signed calibration operator whose absolute expectation recovers the true Expected Calibration Error (ECE) exclusively under globally unidirectional miscalibration. This exposes a fundamental duality between cancellation-prone signed error metrics and robust, binned absolute deviation measures in probability estimation.
gsi_mapping: In GSI Bayesian inference, the Balance score's sign-cancellation flaw mirrors improper posterior aggregation across disjoint parameter manifolds. Conformal prediction sets must rely on absolute ECE rather than signed residuals to guarantee valid coverage probabilities when local over/under-confidence fluctuates across complex feature spaces.
gse_mapping: GSE situational reasoning requires localized state-transition reliability. The Balance score fails because NFL slice probabilities exhibit mixed directional miscalibration. Robust game-state modeling demands binned ECE or isotonic scaling per slice to prevent opposing errors from masking critical calibration drifts.

reasoning_traces.think:
The mathematical spine of this primitive rests on the proposed Balance score, a piecewise per-example function $g(q; p)$ designed to evaluate probability estimation without binning. The authors assert that the absolute value of the average Balance score approximates the true Expected Calibration Error (ECE). However, rigorous derivation reveals this identity holds strictly under the assumption that the sign of $(q - p)$ is constant across the probability range—meaning the model must be globally overconfident or globally underconfident. In high-dimensional sports intelligence contexts like GSE, models routinely exhibit mixed directional miscalibration across different situational slices (e.g., overconfident in early-game states, underconfident in late-game states). When the miscalibration curve crosses zero, the signed errors in the Balance score cancel out, yielding a deceptively low metric while the true absolute ECE remains high. This cancellation singularity renders the Balance score an invalid replacement for binned ECE. The Brier score decomposition further highlights that while variance and resolution components are robust, relying on a signed mean for calibration ignores the non-linear penalty structure required for proper scoring rules. Consequently, the Balance score acts merely as a redundant, weaker diagnostic that can actively mislead headline reporting. For GSE, maintaining slice-based ECE and reliability diagrams ensures that opposing errors do not mask critical calibration drifts, preserving the epistemic integrity of our probabilistic forecasts.
